summary: Specifies extensions to IS-IS needed for link state routing of protocols running directly over Layer 2, with generic TLVs. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS normally routes IP traffic. This RFC adds two fields to IS-IS so that it can also advertise Ethernet hardware addresses, which is what some Layer-2 switching technologies use to compute paths.

questions: what is the mac reachability tlv
subtitle: Two IS-IS TLVs that let a link state protocol carry Layer-2 MAC addresses.

tldr.problem: Some Layer-2 systems, such as provider backbone bridges, shortest path bridging and overlay transport virtualization, route using MAC addresses carried in a link state protocol. IS-IS had no way to advertise those addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Multi-Topology-Aware Port Capability TLV that announces what a port can do, and a MAC-Reachability TLV that lists the unicast MAC addresses reachable from the router that advertises it.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from April 2011 that has not been obsoleted or updated. The TLVs are deliberately generic, and each Layer-2 technology defines the parts it needs in its own extension document.

facts.label: MT-PORT-CAP TLV
facts.value: IS-IS TLV type 143, carried in Hello PDUs

facts.label: MAC-RI TLV
facts.value: IS-IS TLV type 147, carried in Link State PDUs

facts.value: 5 plus 6 times the number of MAC addresses, in bytes

facts.value: 12 bits, and zero means base topology information

facts.value: 48 bits each, and only unicast addresses are allowed

today: RFC 6165 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The two TLVs it registers are generic; each Layer-2 technology that uses them defines its own sub-TLVs and its own meaning for the confidence field in its own extension document.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
There are a number of systems, for example RBridges, IEEE 802.1aq Shortest Path Bridging and Overlay Transport Virtualization, that use Layer-2 addresses carried in a link state routing protocol, specifically Intermediate System to Intermediate System, to provide true Layer-2 routing. In almost all of those technologies, classical Layer-2 packets are encapsulated with an outer header, and the format of that outer header varies from one technology to another. The outer header is what routes the encapsulated packets to their destination.

Each Intermediate System advertises one or more IS-IS Link State Protocol Data Units with routing information. Each Link State PDU is composed of a fixed header and a number of tuples, each consisting of a Type, a Length and a Value, and such tuples are commonly known as TLVs.

This document specifies a set of TLVs to be added to IS-IS PDUs to support these proposed systems. The TLVs are generic Layer-2 additions, and the specific ones that a given technology needs are defined in the IS-IS technology-specific extensions. This document does not propose any new forwarding mechanisms using the additional information carried within IS-IS.
sections.plainLanguage: When a frame crosses a Layer-2 network it is wrapped in an outer header, and that outer header is what carries it to the right place. The wrapping is different in every technology, but the routing information underneath can be shared, so this RFC adds generic fields to IS-IS that the individual technologies fill in as they need.

sections.title: The Multi-Topology-Aware Port Capability TLV
sections.content:
The Multi-Topology-aware Port Capability, abbreviated MT-PORT-CAP, is IS-IS TLV type 143. Its format is a one-byte Type field set to 143, a one-byte Length field giving the total number of bytes in the value field including the length of the sub-TLVs it carries, then a two-byte field holding four reserved bits and a 12-bit Topology Identifier, then the sub-TLVs themselves in a variable number of bytes.

The four reserved bits must be sent as zero and ignored on receipt. The Topology Identifier is a 12-bit field containing the MT ID of the topology being announced, and when it is set to zero it implies that the TLV is being used to carry base topology information.

The sub-TLVs in the value field are formatted as described in RFC 5305, and they are defined in the technology-specific documents.

The MT-PORT-CAP TLV may occur multiple times and is carried within an IS-IS Hello PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: This field goes in the Hello packets that neighbours exchange. It says which topology the port is on and then carries whatever details that particular Layer-2 technology wants to announce about it.

sections.title: The MAC-Reachability TLV
sections.content:
The MAC-Reachability TLV, abbreviated MAC-RI, is IS-IS TLV type 147. Its format is a one-byte Type field set to 147, a one-byte Length field giving the total number of bytes in the value field, a two-byte Topology-id/Nickname field, a one-byte Confidence field, a two-byte field holding four reserved bits and a 12-bit VLAN-ID, and then the MAC addresses themselves, each six bytes long.

Depending on the technology in which it is used, the Topology-id/Nickname field carries the topology-id or the nickname. When it is set to zero this implies that the MAC addresses are reachable across all topologies, or across all nicknames, of the originating Intermediate System.

The Confidence field carries an 8-bit quantity indicating the confidence level in the MAC addresses being transported. Whether the field is used, and its semantics if it is, are defined further by the specific protocol using Layer-2 IS-IS. If it is not used, it must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The four reserved bits must be sent as zero and ignored on receipt. The VLAN-ID field carries a 12-bit VLAN identifier that is valid for all subsequent MAC addresses in the TLV, or the value zero if no VLAN is specified. Each MAC(i) entry is the 48-bit MAC address reachable from the Intermediate System that is announcing the TLV.

The MAC-RI TLV is carried in a standard Link State PDU. It can be carried multiple times in an LSP and in multiple LSPs. It must contain only unicast addresses. The manner in which these TLVs are generated by the various Layer-2 routing technologies, and the manner in which they are consumed, are detailed in the technology-specific documents. In most of the technologies these MAC-RI TLVs translate into populating the hardware with these entries, together with the appropriate next-hop information as derived from the advertising Intermediate System.
sections.plainLanguage: This field goes in the link state packets. It lists the hardware addresses that can be reached from the router sending it, along with the VLAN they sit in, and receivers normally load those entries into their forwarding hardware with a next hop taken from the same advertisement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document adds no additional security risks to IS-IS, nor does it provide any additional security for IS-IS.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new. The security of IS-IS as a whole is unchanged by these two fields, and they do not add any protection of their own.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies a set of new IS-IS TLVs, the Port-Capability TLV of type 143 and the MAC-Reachability TLV of type 147, and lists them in the IS-IS TLV codepoint registry.

The MT-Port-Cap-TLV of type 143 is carried in Hello PDUs and not in Link State PDUs or Sequence Numbers PDUs. The MAC-RI TLV of type 147 is carried in Link State PDUs and not in Hello PDUs or Sequence Numbers PDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of IS-IS TLV numbers and records which kind of packet each one travels in. Two numbers are added here, one for Hello packets and one for link state packets.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total number of bytes in the value field, including the sub-TLVs it carries.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Four reserved bits. Must be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Topology Identifier
fields.desc: The MT ID of the topology being announced. Zero means base topology information.

fields.name: Sub-TLVs
fields.desc: Sub-TLVs formatted as in RFC 5305, defined in the technology-specific documents. The number of bytes is variable.

viz.caption: The MAC-Reachability TLV, shown with two MAC addresses

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total number of bytes in the value field, which is 5 plus 6 times the number of MAC addresses.

fields.name: Topology-id/Nickname
fields.desc: The topology-id or the nickname, depending on the technology. Zero means reachable across all topologies or nicknames.

fields.name: Confidence
fields.desc: An 8-bit confidence level in the MAC addresses. If unused it must be set to zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: RESV
fields.desc: Four reserved bits. Must be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: VLAN-ID
fields.desc: A 12-bit VLAN identifier valid for all subsequent MAC addresses in this TLV, or zero if no VLAN is specified.

fields.name: MAC (1)
fields.desc: A 48-bit unicast MAC address reachable from the Intermediate System announcing this TLV.

fields.name: MAC (N)
fields.desc: Further MAC addresses follow, each 6 bytes long.

items.label: MT-Port-Cap-TLV
items.desc: Carried in Hello PDUs. Announces the capabilities of a port for one topology.

items.label: MAC-RI TLV
items.desc: Carried in Link State PDUs. Lists the unicast MAC addresses reachable from the advertising router.
